title: What is Data Science and the Data Scientist Role
summary: Data science is the practice of extracting insights and building predictions from data to support decisions. A data scientist blends three skill sets: statistics to reason about data, programming to manipulate it, and domain and communication skills
content:
# What is Data Science and the Data Scientist Role ##### The ₹2 crore question nobody could answer A mid-sized pharmacy chain in Nagpur had 47 stores and a problem. Some stores ran out of common medicines by Thursday; others had stock expiring on the shelf. The owner estimated the combined cost of stockouts and expiry at around ₹2 crore a year. He had data — three years of every sale, in a billing system nobody had ever exported. He hired an analyst who produced a beautiful monthly dashboard: sales by store, top-selling items, revenue trends. It was accurate. It changed nothing, because it answered *what happened* and the owner needed to know *what to order next Tuesday*. The person who eventually solved it did three things the analyst had not. She reframed the business problem ("reduce stockouts and expiry") into a prediction problem ("forecast weekly demand per medicine per store"). She built a model that used seasonality, local festivals, and nearby-store patterns. And — the part people underestimate — she convinced 47 store managers to trust a number produced by a computer instead of their own intuition. That combination is data science. Not the model. The whole path from a messy business question to a decision someone actually acts on. ##### What data science actually is The textbook definition — extracting knowledge and insights from data using scientific methods — is true and unhelpfully vague. A more useful framing is three overlapping skill sets: ```mermaid mindmap root((Data Science)) Statistics Is this pattern real or noise? How confident should I be? What causes what? Programming Get the data Clean the data Build and run models Domain and communication Which question matters? Will anyone act on this? How do I explain it? ``` **Statistics** is how you reason under uncertainty. Sales rose 8% after a change — is that the change, or is it just a good month? Without statistical thinking you will confidently report noise as insight, and eventually someone will make an expensive decision based on it. **Programming** is how you touch the data at all. Real datasets are too big for a spreadsheet, arrive in awkward formats, and need the same cleaning repeated every week. Code makes that repeatable. **Domain knowledge and communication** is what separates a useful data scientist from an expensive one. Knowing that pharmacy demand spikes before a long weekend, or that a "customer_id" of `0` in this system means "walk-in, not registered", is worth more than a better algorithm. And an insight nobody understands or trusts has zero value — a slightly worse model that a store manager will actually follow beats a perfect model they ignore. Most people entering the field have one of these three and assume the other two are secondary. They are not. The interesting work lives where they overlap. ##### Data science vs data analytics vs ML engineering These titles are used loosely, and job ads mix them freely. But the underlying roles differ in a way worth understanding before you choose what to study. | | Data Analyst | Data Scientist | ML Engineer | |---|---|---|---| | Core question | What happened? | What will happen, and why? | How do we run this reliably at scale? | | Typical output | Dashboard, report, SQL query | Model, experiment, recommendation | Deployed service, pipeline | | Main tools | SQL, Excel, Power BI, Tableau | Python, Pandas, scikit-learn, statistics | Python, Docker, Kubernetes, cloud | | Time horizon | Past and present | Near future | Continuous operation | | Depth in | Business context, visualisation | Statistics, modelling, experiment design | Software engineering, infrastructure | Made concrete with one company — a food delivery app in Pune: - The **data analyst** reports that order cancellations rose from 4.1% to 6.3% last month, and breaks it down by city, hour and restaurant category. Someone now knows there is a problem and roughly where. - The **data scientist** investigates *why*, discovers that cancellations spike when the estimated delivery time exceeds 38 minutes, builds a model predicting which orders are at risk, and designs an experiment to test whether showing a more honest estimate reduces cancellations. They quantify the expected impact. - The **ML engineer** takes that model and makes it serve 4,000 predictions a second at under 50 milliseconds, with monitoring that alerts when it degrades, and a rollback path when a new version misbehaves. All three are needed. In a small Indian startup one person often does all three — which is a genuinely good way to learn, if exhausting. In a large company they are separate teams. A fourth title you will see is **data engineer**: the person who builds the pipelines that make data available in the first place. Without them, everyone else is querying a system that goes down every Tuesday. ##### The lifecycle: CRISP-DM Beginners imagine data science as "get data, train model, done." The reality is a loop, and the standard description of it is **CRISP-DM** (Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining). It is from 1999 and it has aged remarkably well. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[1. Business Understanding
What decision are we improving?] --> B[2. Data Understanding
What do we have? Is it any good?] B --> C[3. Data Preparation
Clean, join, engineer features] C --> D[4. Modeling
Train, tune, compare] D --> E[5. Evaluation
Does this meet the business goal?] E --> F[6. Deployment
Put it where decisions happen] E -->|Goal not met| A B -->|Data can't answer this| A F --> G[Monitor] --> A ``` The single most important arrow is the one from Evaluation back to Business Understanding. Projects fail far more often from solving the wrong problem than from a weak model. The proportions surprise people. In practice, steps 2 and 3 — understanding and preparing data — take **60 to 80 percent** of the time. Modelling is often a single afternoon. If a course spends 90% of its time on algorithms, it is preparing you for 10% of the job. Applying it to the pharmacy case: Business Understanding was reframing "our stock is a mess" into a forecastable question. Data Understanding was discovering that store 23's data was unusable for six months because the billing machine's clock was wrong. Data Preparation was normalising 11,000 medicine names typed differently across stores. Modelling was two days. Deployment was a weekly order sheet emailed to each manager — no API, no dashboard, just a sheet they would actually use. ##### Types of data You will hear data described in three buckets, and the distinction determines what tools you reach for. **Structured data** lives in rows and columns with a defined type per column — database tables, CSVs, spreadsheets. A transaction table with `date`, `store_id`, `medicine_code`, `quantity`, `amount_inr` is structured. This is the majority of business data and where most beginner work happens. **Unstructured data** has no predefined shape — text, images, audio, video. Customer complaint emails, product photographs, call-centre recordings. It is estimated to be the large majority of all data generated, and it needs different techniques (natural language processing, computer vision) to work with. **Semi-structured data** sits between: it has organisational markers but no rigid table shape. JSON API responses, XML, log files. Very common in modern systems. ```python # Structured — a table import pandas as pd sales = pd.DataFrame({ "date": ["2026-07-01", "2026-07-01", "2026-07-02"], "store_id": [12, 23, 12], "medicine": ["Paracetamol 500", "Amoxicillin 250", "Paracetamol 500"], "units": [140, 32, 155], }) # Semi-structured — JSON, nested and variable order = { "order_id": "ORD-88134", "store": {"id": 12, "city": "Nagpur"}, "items": [ {"medicine": "Paracetamol 500", "units": 2}, {"medicine": "ORS sachet", "units": 5}, ], "notes": "Customer asked for generic alternative", # unstructured, inside structure } # Unstructured — free text complaint = "The delivery was 2 hours late and the strip was damaged." ``` Notice the `notes` field: real data mixes all three. That JSON has structure at the top, a nested list in the middle, and free text at the bottom. Handling that mixture gracefully is a core practical skill. Data also differs in how it arrives — **batch** (a file every night) versus **streaming** (events arriving continuously) — and in whether it is **first-party** (yours), **third-party** (bought), or **public** (open data portals like data.gov.in, which is a genuinely good source for practice projects with Indian context). ##### Tools and where to start The ecosystem is large and the temptation is to learn all of it. Do not. Here is the honest ordering: | Stage | Learn | Why | |---|---|---| | Foundation | Python, SQL | Non-negotiable. Every job needs both. | | Core analysis | Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib | 80% of daily work | | Modelling | scikit-learn, statistics | The actual data science | | Sharing | Jupyter, Git, Markdown | How work becomes reviewable | | Later | Cloud, Spark, deep learning, dashboards | Specialise once you know what you need | SQL deserves emphasis because beginners consistently under-rate it. In most companies the data lives in a database, and the fastest path to an answer is a query, not a Python script. Interviewers know this and test it. Skip, for now: deep learning frameworks (you will not need them for tabular business problems), big-data tooling (your data fits in memory), and the newest library announced last week. ##### Career paths and what to expect Common entry points in India, roughly in order of accessibility: data analyst, business analyst, junior data scientist, ML engineer, and increasingly, AI/GenAI engineer. Analyst roles are the most common first job and a completely respectable route — many strong data scientists started by writing SQL for a business team and learning the domain deeply. Progression typically runs analyst → data scientist → senior → lead, with a fork toward either management or deep specialisation (ML engineering, research, platform). Compensation varies enormously by city and company type; product companies and global capability centres in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune pay substantially more than services firms, and the gap widens with experience. The realistic advice: your first job matters less than what you build in it. Domain knowledge compounds. Someone with three years of retail data science is far more valuable to a retailer than a generalist with three years of tutorials. ##### Common mistakes - Starting with algorithms instead of with the business question. - Believing the job is 80% modelling when it is 80% data wrangling. - Learning six libraries shallowly instead of Python and SQL properly. - Skipping statistics because the library computes it for you. - Optimising a metric nobody asked for — accuracy when the business cares about cost. - Ignoring the domain, and so not noticing that a value is impossible. - Building a dashboard when someone needed a decision. - Assuming clean tutorial data resembles real data. It does not. - Never asking "what will you do differently once you know this?" - Treating communication as a soft skill rather than the thing that determines impact. ##### Hands-on Find three real data science job postings — one analyst, one data scientist, one ML engineer — from Indian companies. List every tool, skill and responsibility mentioned, then map each one to a CRISP-DM stage. You will notice quickly that the postings cluster around different stages, and that Python, SQL and communication appear in all three. That table is a better curriculum than any course syllabus. Then write your one-page problem overview. Pick a domain you genuinely find interesting — cricket, healthcare, local transport, agriculture — and write: the decision someone makes today (and how they make it now), the question a model could answer, what data you would need and where it might come from, what could go wrong with that data, how you would know if the model was useful, and who would have to change their behaviour for it to matter. Keep it to one page. That last question is the one that separates a project idea from a project that works. Finally, write your own explanation of the three roles with a concrete example of each, using a business you know. Explaining it in your own words is how you find out whether you actually understand it. ##### Key takeaways - Data science is the intersection of statistics, programming, and domain plus communication — not any one of them. - Analysts explain the past, data scientists predict and explain why, ML engineers make it run reliably. - CRISP-DM's loop is real, and the arrow back from Evaluation to Business Understanding is the most-used one. - Understanding and preparing data takes 60–80% of the time; modelling is rarely the bottleneck. - Learn Python and SQL properly before anything else, and always ask what decision your work will change.
